paragraphs.text: In the deep ocean, where sunlight never reaches, most animals make their own light. Fish, squid, shrimp and jellyfish flash, glow and shimmer in the darkness, and some estimates suggest that around three-quarters of the animals living in the open ocean at depths of several hundred metres are able to produce light. On land the ability is much rarer, found in fireflies, some fungi, a few worms and insects, but in the sea it is so widespread that it may be the most common form of communication on the planet. Biologists call it bioluminescence, and it has evolved independently dozens of times. The light ranges from steady glows to brief flashes lasting a fraction of a second, and on land fireflies are by far the best-known example.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The chemistry behind most living light is broadly similar. A molecule known as a luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called a luciferase, and the reaction releases energy as light rather than heat. The light is so efficient that it produces almost no warmth, which is why it is sometimes called cold light. The particular luciferins and luciferases differ between groups of organisms, which is one of the reasons scientists believe the ability arose separately many times rather than being inherited from a single ancestor. Some animals do not make their own luciferin at all but obtain it from their food. The colour of the light depends on the structure of the molecules involved.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Many creatures do not produce light themselves but house bacteria that do. Certain fish carry colonies of glowing bacteria in special organs beneath their eyes or along their bellies, supplying them with nutrients and a place to live in exchange for light. A small squid found in shallow Pacific waters hosts bacteria in an organ on its underside, and can control how much of their light escapes through a kind of shutter. Each morning it expels most of the bacteria into the sea, and the remaining population grows back by nightfall. The relationship is so close that the young squid cannot develop the organ properly unless the right bacteria colonise it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The uses of living light are remarkably varied. Some deep-sea fish dangle a glowing lure in front of their mouths to attract prey. Others produce flashes to startle predators or release clouds of glowing material to confuse them while they escape. Fireflies use patterns of flashes to find mates, and each species has its own code, a system that some predatory fireflies exploit by imitating the signals of another species and eating the males that respond. Some animals even use light as camouflage. Some shrimp spit out glowing clouds that leave a predator snapping at light while the shrimp itself swims away.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: This last use, known as counter-illumination, is one of the most elegant. In the middle depths of the ocean, faint light from the surface still filters down, and an animal swimming above a predator appears as a dark shadow against it. Many fish and squid avoid this by producing light on their undersides that matches the brightness and colour of the light from above, so that they seem to disappear. Some species can adjust their output as the light changes during the day, a feat of precision that engineers have studied with interest. Experiments in which fish were placed under artificial lights of changing brightness showed how quickly they adjust.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Most living light is blue or green, because these colours travel furthest through seawater, and many deep-sea animals can see only these colours. A few fish, however, produce red light, which most other animals in the deep cannot detect. These fish can use it like a private searchlight, illuminating prey that remain unaware they are being watched. Some also possess eye pigments that allow them to see their own red light, an adaptation that appears to have evolved partly by incorporating a substance derived from chlorophyll in their food. Researchers are still debating how these fish first acquired the ability.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Bioluminescence has become an important tool in laboratories. A protein that glows green, first found in a jellyfish, can be attached to other proteins so that researchers can see where they are and when they are active inside living cells. The discovery earned a Nobel Prize and transformed cell biology. The enzymes of fireflies are used in tests that detect tiny amounts of living material, for example to check whether surfaces in food factories and hospitals have been properly cleaned. Glowing proteins are now routinely used to track the spread of cancer cells in laboratory animals.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Much remains unknown about light in the deep sea, because studying it is difficult. The bright lamps of research vehicles can blind animals adapted to darkness and interrupt their behaviour, and many species are damaged when brought to the surface. Newer cameras sensitive enough to film in near-darkness, using red light that the animals cannot see, are beginning to reveal how often and in what ways they signal to each other. What they show suggests that the dark ocean is far from dark, and that its inhabitants are constantly communicating in a language of light. Some species have been filmed for the first time only in the past few years.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: The price of electricity from sunlight has fallen more dramatically than almost anyone predicted. In the early 1980s, a solar panel capable of producing one watt of power cost the equivalent of dozens of dollars; today it costs a small fraction of one dollar, and in many sunny regions solar farms now generate the cheapest electricity ever produced. This transformation came not from a single discovery but from steady improvements in manufacturing, larger factories and the enormous growth in demand that followed government support in several countries. Few energy technologies have changed so quickly, and solar power is now the fastest-growing source of electricity in many countries.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Almost all the panels installed today are made from silicon, the same material used in computer chips. When light strikes a thin wafer of specially treated silicon, it frees electrons that can flow as an electric current. The principle was demonstrated in the 1950s, and the first practical silicon cells were used to power satellites, where their high cost mattered less than their reliability. For decades, solar power on Earth remained too expensive for anything except remote uses such as lighthouses and road signs far from the electricity grid. Early cells converted only a few per cent of the sunlight that fell on them into electricity. Silicon itself is abundant, since it is made from ordinary sand, but purifying it requires a great deal of energy.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Silicon has a fundamental limit. A single layer of silicon can convert at most about a third of the energy in sunlight into electricity, because some colours of light carry too little energy to free an electron and others carry more than is needed, with the excess lost as heat. The best commercial panels now approach this limit, converting well over a fifth of the sunlight that falls on them. Further large gains will therefore require a different approach rather than simply better silicon. Manufacturers have gained efficiency by making cells that capture light on both sides, using light reflected from the ground.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The most promising candidates are materials called perovskites, named after a mineral with a similar crystal structure. First used in solar cells in 2009, they improved with astonishing speed: within about a decade, their efficiency in the laboratory rose from under four per cent to levels comparable with silicon. Perovskites can be made from solutions at low temperatures, rather than in the energy-intensive furnaces required for silicon, and they can be printed onto flexible surfaces, raising the possibility of solar cells on windows, vehicles and clothing. Laboratories around the world took up the material quickly, and thousands of research papers have been published on it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Their most important use may be in combination with silicon. Because perovskites can be tuned to absorb colours of light that silicon uses poorly, a thin layer placed on top of a silicon cell can capture energy that silicon alone would waste. Such tandem cells have already exceeded the theoretical limit of a single silicon layer in laboratory tests, and several manufacturers are preparing to produce them commercially. Some researchers are also experimenting with cells that stack three or more layers, each tuned to a different part of the spectrum.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The obstacle has been durability. Early perovskite cells degraded within hours or days when exposed to moisture, oxygen, heat or even the light they were meant to capture. Silicon panels, by contrast, are routinely guaranteed to keep most of their performance for twenty-five years or more. Researchers have made considerable progress by protecting the cells with better coatings and adjusting their chemistry, but proving that they will last for decades outdoors requires long tests that cannot be shortened entirely. Some perovskites also contain small amounts of lead, raising concerns about what happens if a panel is damaged or discarded. Several companies claim that their latest designs have passed standard accelerated ageing tests.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Other challenges lie outside the cell itself. The sun shines only during the day and less in winter, so a power system that relies heavily on solar energy needs ways of storing electricity or balancing supply with other sources. In places with a great deal of solar capacity, the price of electricity at midday can fall very low or even below zero on sunny days, reducing the income of the owners of solar farms. Cheaper storage, particularly batteries, is making this problem easier to manage. Some solar farms now include batteries on the same site so that electricity can be sold in the evening.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The history of solar power suggests that predictions about its future should be treated with caution. Forecasts made twenty years ago consistently underestimated how quickly costs would fall and how much would be installed. Whether perovskites follow the same path depends on whether their durability can be proved convincingly, but even if they fail, the continuing improvement of silicon panels and the systems around them means that the sun is likely to supply a much larger share of the electricity of the world in the coming decades. Solar panels themselves will also need to be recycled in growing numbers as early installations reach the end of their lives, which is technically possible but not yet widely practised.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: In every country that carries out organ transplants, far more people need organs than there are organs available, and many patients die while waiting. Most donated organs come from people who have died in circumstances, usually in hospital intensive care units, that allow their organs to be used, and the decision whether to donate typically rests on the wishes of the deceased and the agreement of their family. In recent years a growing number of countries have changed the law so that adults are presumed to have agreed to donate unless they have registered an objection, a system usually called opt-out. Whether this increases the number of organs available is less clear than its supporters often suggest. The shortage is growing as populations age and as transplant techniques improve.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case for opt-out rests partly on a well-documented feature of human behaviour: people tend to stick with whatever option is presented as the default. Surveys in many countries show that a large majority of people support organ donation, yet far fewer have registered as donors, often simply because they have never got round to it. Clare Morgan, a transplant surgeon, argues that an opt-out system brings the law into line with what most people want, and removes the burden from families who would otherwise have to guess the wishes of a relative at a moment of great distress. Registering is usually simple, but it requires people to think about their own death, which many prefer to avoid.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The evidence on outcomes is mixed. Some countries with opt-out laws have among the highest donation rates in the world, but several of them also invested heavily in other measures at the same time, such as training specialist staff and improving the identification of potential donors in hospitals. Rashid Karimov, a health economist who has compared countries, argues that these organisational changes explain most of the difference. When he examined countries that changed their law without improving their hospital systems, he found little or no increase in donation rates. Comparisons between countries are also complicated by differences in how deaths are recorded and which organs are counted.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: In practice, families remain central even under opt-out laws. In most countries that have adopted the system, doctors still speak to relatives before any organs are removed, and do not proceed if the family objects strongly. This so-called soft opt-out means that the change in the law may matter less than the conversation that takes place at the bedside. Morgan points out that the way this conversation is conducted, and by whom, has a large effect on whether families agree, and that specially trained staff obtain consent far more often than doctors without such training. In some countries the views of the family are formally part of the law; in others they are respected in practice.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Critics raise questions of principle. Ingrid Holt, a bioethicist, argues that consent to something as significant as the removal of organs should be given actively rather than assumed from silence, and that people who are unaware of the law, including those with limited literacy or recent immigrants, may be treated as donors against their wishes. She accepts that the current shortage causes real harm, but maintains that a system of mandated choice, in which everyone must record a decision when applying for a driving licence or other document, would respect autonomy better while still increasing registration. Some countries have adopted mandated choice for certain groups, with mixed results.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Public trust is essential to any system. Tomas Reyes, a sociologist, has found that in some communities, fear that doctors might make less effort to save a registered donor, although unfounded, discourages registration, and that a change to opt-out can increase these fears if it is poorly explained. In one country where the law changed with little public discussion, the number of people registering an objection rose sharply in the following months. Reyes argues that any change in the law must be accompanied by sustained information campaigns, particularly among groups whose trust in the health system is low. Religious leaders have played an important part in some campaigns, explaining that most faiths support donation.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The debate also affects which organs are available and for whom. Patients from some ethnic backgrounds are more likely to need a transplant and less likely to find a well-matched donor, partly because donation rates in their communities are lower. Karimov notes that changes to the law have done little to address this imbalance, which depends far more on engagement with particular communities than on the formal rules of consent. Living donors, who give a kidney or part of a liver, face different questions that the opt-out debate does not address.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The weight of evidence suggests that the choice between opt-in and opt-out matters less than the quality of the system surrounding it. Trained staff, careful conversations with families and public trust appear to have a larger effect on donation rates than the default set by law. Opt-out may help as part of a broader programme, and it has symbolic value in signalling that donation is the normal expectation, but on its own it is unlikely to end the shortage of organs.
paragraphs.label: H
